citation: Keane, Niall. "The Affects of Rhetoric and Reconceiving the Nature of Possibility." In Heidegger on Affect, edited by Christos Hadjioannou, 47-68. Philosophers in Depth. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan, 2019.
thesis: Heidegger's 1924 summer-semester lecture course, Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy (GA 18/BCAP), is the textual soil from which both Being and Time's existential analytic and the later Contributions to Philosophy's critique of the metaphysics of actuality grow. In these early lectures, Heidegger rehabilitates Aristotle's Rhetoric against the Platonic Gorgias reading of rhetoric-as-flattery, recasting rhetoric as a dynamis (potentiality) for disclosing 'what speaks for a matter' rather than a persuasion-technique (techne); this rehabilitation grounds a phenomenological account of logos, pathos, doxa, and being-with-one-another that later underwrites BT's ontology of Dasein and, still later, CP's radical critique of the metaphysical priority of actuality (energeia) over possibility (dynamis).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: States the thesis via Sheehan's charge that later Heidegger's rhetoric is 'over-wrought'; frames the 1924 task as recovering the ground from which Aristotle's basic concepts emerge, disclosed by way of speaking (legein).

sections.title: Rhetoric as dynamis, not techne (unnumbered continuation)
sections.summary: Heidegger's rehabilitation of rhetoric against Plato's Gorgias (463a6-465e1); rhetoric vs. sophistry; rhetoric's psychagogic kinship with dialectic via the Phaedrus (276e5-6).

sections.title: 1 Aristotle's Rhetoric
sections.summary: Endoxic character of rhetoric; pisteis (technical/non-technical); enthymema as rhetorical syllogism; narrow (apodeictic) vs. broad (rhetorical/affective) senses of 'logical'; logos as the fundamental mode of being-in-the-world.

sections.title: 2 Heidegger's Appropriation of Rhetoric
sections.summary: Aristotle read as proto-phenomenologist; disclosedness (Erschlossenheit) vs. uncoveredness (Entdecktheit); the three pisteis entechnoi (ethos/pathos/logos); rhetoric and dialectic as dynameis facilitated by the intellectual virtues (hexeis).

sections.title: 3 Being with Others and Speaking with Others
sections.summary: Rhetoric's hermeneutical core prior to Arendt and Gadamer; hedone read as Befindlichkeit ('self-having'); embodiment and pathos as the ground (Boden) of speaking; koinon/koinonia; doxa as source of everydayness; BT's citation of Aristotle's Rhetoric as 'the first systematic hermeneutic' of being-with (SZ 138).

sections.title: 4 On Actuality and Possibility
sections.summary: Critique of the metaphysical priority of actuality (energeia) over possibility (dynamis), keyed to Metaphysics Theta 1049b13; Dasein's 'who' vs. 'what'; the ontological difference as itself a possibility; CP's attack on the 'modalities'; blocked/submerged possibility as a through-line of Heidegger's corpus.

sections.title: Endnotes and references
sections.summary: Five endnotes (Plato's Phaedrus/Sophist, Bambach on 'appropriate ethos,' P. Christopher Smith's 'de-acoustification' charge) and a four-item bibliography (Kisiel 2005, Michalski 2005, Sheehan 2015, Withy 2015).

readings.claim: Rhetoric is more accurately a dynamis (potentiality) than a techne (craft); the rhetorician discloses 'what speaks for a matter' rather than manipulating appearances.
readings.stance: extends-reading-of (Aristotle's Rhetoric, against the Gorgias reading)

readings.claim: Sophistry is distinguished from rhetoric by its aim to 'conquer the other without knowledge of the matter discussed,' not by any technical feature; sophistry's existence is symptomatic of a basic danger native to Greek being-there.
readings.stance: contests (Gorgias-style collapse of rhetoric into sophistry)

readings.claim: Aristotle's Rhetoric is endoxic, proceeding from established belief (doxa) via pisteis; rhetorical (enthymemic) demonstration is grounded in a shared, affective 'body of proof' (soma tes pisteos), distinct from apodeictic/syllogistic demonstration.
Logos is the fundamental mode of our being-in-the-world -- a disclosive space of appearances corresponding to speaking-with-others, not merely the conceptual grasp of a pre-given world.
Aristotle is a proto-phenomenologist whose Rhetoric anticipates BT's distinction between originary disclosedness (Erschlossenheit) and founded uncoveredness (Entdecktheit).

Of Aristotle's three pisteis entechnoi (ethos, pathos, logos), the third is decisive for Heidegger: legein itself is pistis as 'the basic function of being-there itself,' pre-empting BT's claim that Dasein is both understandingly discursive and affectively disclosive.
Speaking-with-one-another is 'the clue to the uncovering' of Dasein's basic being-in-a-world; rhetoric is a concrete guide to the basic possibility of speaking-with-one-another.

Prior to Arendt and Gadamer, Heidegger drew attention to rhetoric's hermeneutical core: humans are genuinely human only insofar as they exist with others amid matters made interpretatively intelligible in conversation; this is where 'pure phenomenology' becomes 'phenomenological hermeneutics.'

Hedone (pleasure), read by Heidegger as Befindlichkeit ('self-having'), threatens to collapse Aristotle's own hexis/pathos distinction but in fact names a transformative 'awakening' possibility within the everyday.
Affects are not private inner states but the 'ground' (Boden) out of which speaking arises; being-there 'finds itself' (Sichbefinden) primarily through affective disposedness, not cognition.

Without the koinon (the common/communal), Dasein would be like 'fish caught in the stream,' unable to reach authentic self-understanding or project possibilities as its own; being-with-one-another (vs. mere being-alongside) grounds both average/everyday doxastic life and the possibility of authentic self-projection.

BT itself credits Aristotle's Rhetoric as 'the first systematic hermeneutic' of everyday being-with-one-another (SZ 138) -- the strongest textual evidence that the 1924 lectures are BT's own acknowledged root.

Heidegger's critique of the metaphysical priority of actuality (energeia) over possibility (dynamis), keyed against Metaphysics Theta 1049b13, can only be properly understood by returning to the 1924 lectures; BT's claim that possibility is 'higher' than actuality was already contained there, though unrecognizable to BT's first readers.

Dasein's ontological constitution is possibilizing and self-possibilizing, not actualized/present-at-hand presence; Heidegger substitutes the 'who' question for the 'what' question; the ontological difference is itself a possibility only because Dasein's own being possibilizes and performs it.

In CP, the origin and dominance of the metaphysical 'modalities' are more questionable than the traditional interpretation of beings as 'idea'; actuality-as-energeia functions as possibility's and necessity's 'two horns'; the tradition reduces even the not-yet-actual to the order of the actual.

Heidegger's decades-long attack on metaphysical modality, in the name of a deeper historically 'blocked' possibility, is legible across his whole corpus; the 1924 reading of the Rhetoric -- as a 'world negotiating exercise of speaking and hearing together' -- is among its earliest instances.

interlocutors.name: Aristotle -- Rhetoric
interlocutors.role: primary source text; rehabilitated by Heidegger as dynamis-based, non-technical, socially disclosive

interlocutors.name: Aristotle -- Metaphysics Theta (1049b13)
interlocutors.role: target of Heidegger's critique of the priority of actuality over possibility

interlocutors.name: Aristotle -- Prior Analytics and Topics
interlocutors.role: site of the 'one-sided dialectical tendency to posit premises' Heidegger counter-balances with rhetoric

interlocutors.name: Plato -- Gorgias (463a6-465e1)
interlocutors.role: the rejected reading of rhetoric as flattery/technical trickery, against which Heidegger reads Aristotle

interlocutors.name: Plato -- Phaedrus (276e5-6)
interlocutors.role: source of rhetoric's psychagogic kinship with dialectic; more ambivalent toward rhetoric than the endnotes concede

interlocutors.name: Plato -- Sophist (via Heidegger's 1924-25 GA 19/PS lecture course)
interlocutors.role: companion lecture course defining rhetoric as techne, in tension with the Rhetoric course's own analysis

interlocutors.name: Heidegger, Martin -- Being and Time (SZ)
interlocutors.role: the existential analytic Keane argues is retrospectively grounded in the 1924 BCAP lectures

interlocutors.name: Heidegger, Martin -- Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy (GA 18/BCAP, 1924)
interlocutors.role: primary source text for the entire chapter

interlocutors.name: Heidegger, Martin -- Plato's Sophist (GA 19/PS, 1924-25)
interlocutors.role: companion lecture course cited for continuity/tension with the Rhetoric course

interlocutors.name: Heidegger, Martin -- Basic Problems of Phenomenology (GA 24/BP)
interlocutors.role: cited for the ontological difference as a possibility Dasein itself possibilizes

interlocutors.name: Heidegger, Martin -- Contributions to Philosophy (GA 65/CP)
interlocutors.role: later text where the 1924-era critique of actuality/possibility is radicalized into an attack on the metaphysical 'modalities'

interlocutors.name: Sheehan, Thomas (2015)
interlocutors.role: opening interlocutor; charges the later Heidegger's rhetoric as 'over-wrought'/'over-heated,' motivating the return to 1924

interlocutors.name: Michalski, Mark (2005)
interlocutors.role: cited gloss on rhetoric as 'making the thing evident in its substantive character'

interlocutors.name: Kisiel, Theodore (2005)
interlocutors.role: cited on pistis as demonstration going 'directly to the heart' (en-thymos)

interlocutors.name: Withy, Katherine (2015)
interlocutors.role: cited on pathos as involving a responsive 'comportment' (verhalten) toward what touches us as mattering

interlocutors.name: Bambach, Charles (2014)
interlocutors.role: endnote 4 -- glosses Heidegger's early rhetoric-inspired move toward an 'appropriate ethos'

interlocutors.name: Smith, P. Christopher (1995)
interlocutors.role: endnote 5 -- charges Heidegger with 'de-acoustification'/'de-vocalization' of speaking and listening against the backdrop of publicness and fallenness

interlocutors.name: Arendt, Hannah / Gadamer, Hans-Georg (mentioned jointly)
interlocutors.role: later thinkers whose attention to rhetoric's hermeneutical core Heidegger's 1924 lectures are said to anticipate

tensions.axis: rhetoric as disclosive dynamis (Aristotle's Rhetoric, per Heidegger) vs. rhetoric/sophistry as technical persuasion-trickery (Plato's Gorgias)
tensions.note: the chapter's organizing distinction; Heidegger sides with Aristotle against the Gorgias reading, arguably also against the 'sophist' pole of Plato's own Phaedrus/Sophist.

tensions.axis: priority of possibility (Heidegger's own thesis) vs. priority of actuality (the dominant metaphysical tradition, including one strand of Aristotle himself)
tensions.note: explicitly NOT the Aristotle of the Rhetoric, per Keane -- the actuality-priority view stems from Metaphysics Theta, creating an internal tension within Heidegger's own use of Aristotle (endorsing the Rhetoric while rejecting the Metaphysics' modal hierarchy).

tensions.axis: narrow/apodeictic logic (scientific, syllogistic) vs. broad/rhetorical logic (enthymemic, affective, evidentially shared)
tensions.note: the two senses of 'logical' that Keane distinguishes in reading Aristotle's Rhetoric alongside the Prior Analytics/Topics.

tensions.axis: being-with-one-another (Mitsein, disclosive) vs. being situated alongside one another (merely co-present)
tensions.note: Heidegger's own explicit distinction (GA 18: 47; BCAP 33); grounds both everyday doxastic life and authentic self-projection.

tensions.axis: phenomenological method's claim of 'no division between psychic and bodily acts' vs. the subsequent refusal to reduce affect to psycho-physical process
tensions.note: an internal qualification within Heidegger's own 1924 position that Keane flags rather than resolves.
